title: Freelance Referral and Testimonial Kit
description: Turn happy clients into testimonials and referrals without feeling pushy. A timing playbook for when to ask, ten short request emails, prompts that get specific quotes, honest editing and permission rules, a referral tracker, a testimonial log, and a fully worked one-month example.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Referral and Testimonial Kit

Most freelancers get their best clients from people who already liked their
work. Most also never ask, or ask once, awkwardly, months too late. This kit
gives you a simple system: ask at the right moment, make it easy to say yes,
get permission in writing, and keep track so nobody slips through.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `ask-timing-playbook.md` | When to ask, what to ask for, and the five moments that work best |
| `request-emails.md` | Ten short emails: testimonials, referrals, reviews, past-client check-ins, thank-yous |
| `testimonial-prompts.md` | Questions that get specific, useful quotes instead of "great to work with" |
| `permission-and-editing.md` | How to get clear consent, edit quotes honestly, and store the proof |
| `referral-tracker.csv` | Track every ask, every intro, and every thank-you |
| `testimonial-log.csv` | Keep each quote with its source, date, permission, and where it's used |
| `worked-example.md` | One freelancer's full month using the kit, start to finish |

## How to use it in 30 minutes

1. Open `referral-tracker.csv` and list every client you've worked with in
   the last 18 months. Mark how each project ended (happy / neutral / rocky).
2. Read `ask-timing-playbook.md`. Pick the 3-5 "happy" clients whose project
   ended in the last 90 days. They are your first asks.
3. Send email 1 or 2 from `request-emails.md` to each. Attach the questions
   from `testimonial-prompts.md` so they don't face a blank page.
4. When a reply comes in, follow `permission-and-editing.md` before you
   publish anything, and log it in `testimonial-log.csv`.
5. Put a recurring 20-minute slot in your calendar on the first Monday of
   each month to update the tracker and send the next round.

## Ground rules

- Only publish words a real client actually wrote or said, with their OK.
- Never offer payment or discounts in exchange for a positive review. A
  thank-you after a referral turns into work is fine; buying praise is not,
  and many review platforms and consumer-protection rules prohibit it.
- If someone says no or doesn't reply after one follow-up, let it go.
  Nobody owes you a testimonial, and the relationship is worth more.
files.ask-timing-playbook.md:
# When to Ask: The Timing Playbook

The single biggest factor in getting a yes is *when* you ask. Ask while the
good result is fresh and the client still feels it.

## The five best moments

### 1. Right after a visible win (best)
The site launched, the campaign beat its target, the report was praised by
their boss. The client is already telling people about it. Ask within 48
hours.

> Signal to watch for: the client sends you a message with "thank you",
> "amazing", "the team loves it", or forwards you praise from someone else.

### 2. At the project wrap-up
Your final handover call or email. Add the ask as the last item, after the
deliverables and the invoice are settled. Never put the ask in the same
email as an overdue invoice reminder.

### 3. When they come back for more
A repeat booking is proof they valued the first round. Before starting the
new work: "Before we kick off, would you be open to a two-line testimonial
about the last project?"

### 4. 30-90 days after a project, when results show up
Some work (SEO, copy, systems, training) only proves itself later. Put a
reminder in the tracker to check in and ask how it's going. If the answer is
good news, that's your testimonial.

### 5. When they refer someone unprompted
Thank them first (see email 8). A client who already referred you is the
easiest yes for a written testimonial.

## When NOT to ask

- While an invoice is overdue or a dispute is open.
- In the middle of a project, before anything is delivered.
- When the project ended rocky, even if it was "fine" in the end. Ask for
  feedback instead (email 6) and learn from it.
- More than twice. One ask, one gentle follow-up, then stop.

## What to ask for (pick one per email)

| Ask | Effort for the client | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| A short written quote (2-4 sentences) | Low | Your website, proposals |
| A public review on a platform | Medium (they need an account) | Being found by strangers |
| A referral to one named type of person | Low-medium | New work fast |
| A short case study call (15 min) | Medium | Your strongest projects |
| Permission to name them as a client | Very low | Logo/client list |

Ask for one thing at a time. Two asks in one email cuts your reply rate.

## Make referrals specific

"Let me know if you know anyone who needs help" gets nothing. Name the
person you want:

- Weak: "If you know anyone who needs a designer..."
- Strong: "I'm taking on two more small bakeries or cafes in the spring who
  need a menu and signage refresh. If another owner comes to mind, I'd love
  an intro."

A specific description lets the client's brain search for one name instead
of everyone they know.

## Monthly rhythm (20 minutes)

1. Open `referral-tracker.csv`. Sort by `next_action_date`.
2. Send anything due today.
3. Add any project that finished this month.
4. Log replies and update `testimonial-log.csv`.
5. Send a thank-you for every intro that happened, whether or not it turned
   into work.
files.request-emails.md:
# Request Emails

Ten short emails. Replace everything in [brackets]. Keep them short: the
shorter the ask, the higher the reply rate. Send from your normal email,
not a mass-mail tool.

---

## 1. Testimonial request, right after a win

**Subject:** Quick favour?

Hi [Name],

I'm really glad [the launch / the report / the result] landed so well.

Would you be open to writing two or three sentences about working together?
I'd use it on my website and in proposals. A few prompts below in case
they help, but anything in your own words is perfect:

- What was the situation before we started?
- What changed after?
- Would you recommend me, and to whom?

No pressure at all, and if now's a busy week, whenever suits.

Thanks,
[Your name]

---

## 2. Testimonial request at wrap-up

**Subject:** Wrapping up [project name]

Hi [Name],

Everything's handed over: [one-line summary of what was delivered]. Thanks
for being great to work with.

One last thing: if you were happy with how it went, a short testimonial
would help me a lot. Two or three sentences is plenty. I'll send you the
final version before anything goes live.

[Your name]

---

## 3. Gentle follow-up (send once, 7-10 days later)

**Subject:** Re: Quick favour?

Hi [Name], just floating this back up in case it got buried. If it's not a
good time, no problem at all. I'll stop nudging!

[Your name]

---

## 4. Referral request, specific

**Subject:** Small ask

Hi [Name],

I've got room for [number] new [type of client] projects starting [month].
The sweet spot is [one-line description: size, industry, problem].

If someone like that comes to mind, I'd be grateful for an intro. A
one-line email copying us both is perfect, and I'll take it from there.

Thanks either way,
[Your name]

---

## 5. Public review request

**Subject:** Would you leave a quick review?

Hi [Name],

Most of my new clients find me through [platform]. If you have two minutes,
an honest review there would make a real difference. You can find my page
by searching "[your business name]" on [platform].

Thanks so much,
[Your name]

> Note: ask for an *honest* review, never a "5-star" one, and don't offer
> anything in return.

---

## 6. Feedback request (for neutral or rocky projects)

**Subject:** What could I have done better?

Hi [Name],

Now that [project] is finished, I'd really value your honest take. What's
one thing that worked and one thing I could have done better? A couple of
lines is plenty. I use this to improve how I work.

[Your name]

---

## 7. Past-client check-in (3-12 months later)

**Subject:** How's [the thing we made] doing?

Hi [Name],

It's been [time] since we [launched / finished X]. I was curious how it's
holding up. Has [the result you were aiming for] stuck?

No agenda, just interested. If anything needs a tweak, happy to help.

[Your name]

---

## 8. Thank-you after a referral

**Subject:** Thank you for the intro to [Referred name]

Hi [Name],

Thank you for connecting me with [Referred name]. That meant a lot.
[We've got a call booked / We're starting next month / It wasn't the right
fit this time, but I appreciated it all the same.]

[Your name]

---

## 9. Send the edited quote for approval

**Subject:** Your testimonial: OK to use?

Hi [Name],

Thank you for this! I trimmed it slightly for length. Here's the version
I'd like to use:

> "[Edited quote]"
> - [Name], [Role], [Company]

Is it OK to use this on my website and in proposals, with your name, role
and company as shown? If you'd prefer just first name, or no company,
tell me and I'll change it.

[Your name]

---

## 10. Client list / logo permission

**Subject:** OK to list you as a client?

Hi [Name],

Would it be OK to list [Company] among the clients I've worked with on my
website? Just the name [and logo], no project details. Totally fine to say
no.

[Your name]
files.testimonial-prompts.md:
# Testimonial Prompts

A blank page produces "Great to work with, highly recommend!" That's kind,
but it doesn't sell anything. Specific details do. Send clients three or
four of these questions. They answer whichever ones they like.

## The core four (use these by default)

1. What was going on before we worked together? What was the problem or
   the worry?
2. Was there anything that made you hesitate about hiring someone for this?
3. What changed after? A number, a reaction, or a saved headache all count.
4. Who would you recommend me to?

Question 2 is the secret one. Answers like "I worried it would take
forever" or "I'd been burned by a freelancer before" are exactly what your
next prospect is worried about too.

## Extra prompts by type of work

**Design / creative**
- How did your customers or team react to the new [design]?
- What was it like giving feedback during the project?

**Writing / content**
- Did the [copy / articles] save you time or change any numbers you track?
- How much editing did you need to do on what was delivered?

**Development / technical**
- Was anything easier, faster or more reliable afterwards?
- How was communication when things got technical?

**Consulting / strategy / coaching**
- What decision or action did you take because of our work?
- What would you tell someone on the fence about hiring me?

## Turning a call into a quote

Some clients would rather talk. Book 10-15 minutes, ask the core four, and
take notes in their words, not yours. Then:

1. Pull 2-4 sentences that are mostly their exact words.
2. Fix only grammar and filler ("um", "you know").
3. Send it back with email 9 for approval.

Never add claims they didn't make. If they said "it felt faster", don't
write "load times dropped 40%".

## Before and after examples

**Generic (fine, but weak):**
> "Sam was great to work with. Very professional. Would recommend."

**Specific (from the core four):**
> "We'd tried to redo our menu twice and given up both times. Sam got it
> done in three weeks with almost no back-and-forth, and customers started
> commenting on it the first weekend. If you run a small cafe and keep
> putting off the menu, just hire Sam."

The second one answers the next client's real question: *will this work
for someone like me?*
files.permission-and-editing.md:
# Permission and Editing

A testimonial is only an asset if you can use it with confidence. These
habits keep it honest and keep you safe. This is general good practice,
not legal advice. If you work in a regulated field (finance, health, law),
check your own professional rules about testimonials.

## Get permission in writing

Before anything goes public, confirm by email (email 9 does this):

- **The exact wording** you'll publish
- **The name format**: full name, first name only, initials, or anonymous
- **Role and company**: shown or not
- **Where** you'll use it: website, proposals, social media, portfolio
- **Photo or logo**: only if they say yes separately

A "sure, go ahead" reply to that email is your record. Save it (see the
log below).

## Editing rules

You may:
- Fix spelling, grammar and punctuation
- Cut filler words and repetition
- Shorten to the strongest 2-4 sentences
- Use "..." where you cut words from the middle of a sentence

You may not:
- Add words, numbers or claims the client didn't say
- Combine quotes from different people into one
- Change the meaning, even slightly
- Keep using a quote after the client asks you to remove it

**Rule of thumb:** if the client would read the edited version and say "I
didn't say that," it's wrong.

## When a client asks you to take it down

Remove it everywhere within a few days, no questions asked. Mark it
`withdrawn` in `testimonial-log.csv` with the date so you don't
accidentally reuse it in an old proposal template.

## Storing the proof

For each testimonial keep:

1. The original message (email, chat export, or call notes)
2. The approval email
3. A row in `testimonial-log.csv`

A simple folder named `testimonials/` with one subfolder per client is
enough.

## Reviews on public platforms

- Ask for an honest review, never a specific star rating.
- Don't offer discounts, gifts or payment for reviews.
- Don't write reviews for clients to "just approve".
- Don't ask friends or family to post as if they were clients.

Platforms remove reviews (and sometimes accounts) that break their rules,
and in many countries fake or paid reviews are against consumer-protection
law.

## Referral thank-yous

Saying thank you after a referral is always fine. If you'd like to give a
gift or a referral fee, be upfront about it with both people. A small
thank-you after the fact (a card, a coffee) is different from paying for
praise. Never tie it to what someone says about you.

files.worked-example.md:
# Worked Example: One Month With the Kit

Sam is a freelance graphic designer who works mostly with small hospitality
and wellness businesses. Sam has had eight clients in the past 18 months
and zero testimonials on the website. All names here are invented for the
example.

## Week 1: Build the list (25 minutes)

Sam lists all eight clients in `referral-tracker.csv` and marks how each
ended:

- 5 happy
- 2 neutral (one had a tight deadline, one went quiet near the end)
- 1 rocky (scope arguments, paid late)

Of the five happy clients, three finished in the last 90 days. Those are the
first asks. The two neutral clients get the feedback email (email 6). The
rocky client gets nothing.

## Week 1: Send the first round

- **Harbour Bakery** (launched new menu 10 days ago, owner said "customers
  love it"): email 1, testimonial request after a win, with the core four
  prompts.
- **Linden Yoga** (finished 3 weeks ago, already rebooked for spring):
  email 4, specific referral ask: "two more small studios who need a
  timetable and poster refresh".
- **Northgate Physio** (finished 3 months ago, brochure goal was more
  bookings): email 7, results check-in. No ask yet.

## Week 2: Replies

- Harbour Bakery replies with five sentences. Sam trims to three, fixes
  one typo, and sends email 9 for approval. Owner says "Perfect, first name
  only please." Sam saves the approval email and logs T001.
- Linden Yoga's manager introduces Sam to a second studio by email. Sam
  sends email 8 the same day and books a discovery call.
- Northgate Physio: no reply yet. Next action set for 9 days later.
- Neutral client #1 replies to the feedback email: "the timeline felt
  rushed". Sam adds a note to build in a buffer week on future quotes.

## Week 3: Follow-ups

- Northgate Physio replies: new patient enquiries are up and two mentioned
  the brochure. Sam replies with thanks, then a week later sends email 1
  asking for a short testimonial, quoting the client's own words back as a
  starting point.
- Sam sends email 10 to Harbour Bakery asking to list the business name on
  the client page. Yes.

## Week 4: Results

| Metric | Before | After 1 month |
|---|---|---|
| Testimonials on website | 0 | 2 approved, 1 pending |
| Clients listed by name | 0 | 3 |
| Referral intros | 0 | 1 (call booked) |
| Feedback notes | 0 | 1 actionable change |
| Time spent | - | About 2 hours total |

Sam's new proposal template now opens with the Harbour Bakery quote, because
it answers the question every small cafe owner has: *will this work for
someone like me?*

## What Sam does next month

- First Monday: open the tracker, sort by `next_action_date`.
- Ask the remaining two happy clients from 6-18 months ago (email 7 first,
  then email 1 if the reply is warm).
- Send one more specific referral ask to the newest happy client.
- Keep the rocky client off the list.
